metadata.title: A Kähler Structure on Cartan Spaces

nodes.name: Vertical distribution on $T^{\ast}M$
nodes.statement: The kernel $V_{(x,p)}$ of the differential $d\pi^{\ast}:T_{(x,p)}T^{\ast}M\rightarrow T_xM$ is called the vertical subspace of $T_{(x,p)}T^{\ast}M$ and the mapping $(x,p)\rightarrow V_{(x,p)}$ is a regular distribution on $T^{\ast}M$ called the vertical distribution. This is integrable with the leaves $T^{\ast}_xM$, $x\in M$ and is locally spanned by $\dot{\partial}^i$.
nodes.statement_short: The kernel of $d\pi^{\ast}$ is the vertical subspace; the resulting regular distribution is integrable with leaves $T^{\ast}_xM$.

nodes.name: Liouville vector field and Liouville 1-form
nodes.statement: The vector field $C^{\ast}=p_i\dot{\partial}^i$ is called the Liouville vector field and $\omega=p_idx^i$ is called the Liouville 1-form on $T^{\ast}M$.

nodes.name: Horizontal-vertical decomposition of $T_{(x,p)}T^{\ast}M$
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} T_{(x,p)}T^{\ast}M=N_{(x,p)}\oplus V_{(x,p)}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Nonlinear connection (horizontal distribution)
nodes.statement: The horizontal distribution is taken as being locally spanned by the local vector fields \begin{equation} \delta_i:=\partial_i+N_{ij}(x,p)\dot{\partial}^j. \end{equation} The horizontal distribution is called also a nonlinear connection on $T^{\ast}M$ and the functions $(N_{ij})$ are called the local coefficients of this nonlinear connection.
nodes.statement_short: The horizontal distribution spanned by $\delta_i=\partial_i+N_{ij}\dot{\partial}^j$ is called a nonlinear connection, with local coefficients $(N_{ij})$.

nodes.name: Cartan structure and Cartan space
nodes.statement: A Cartan structure on $M$ is a function $K:T^{\ast}M\longrightarrow [0,\infty)$ which has the following properties: (i) $K$ is $C^{\infty}$ on $T^{\ast}M_0=T^{\ast}M-\{0\}$; (ii) $K(x,\lambda p)=\lambda K(x,p)$ for all $\lambda>0$ and (iii) the $n\times n$ matrix $(g^{ij})$, where $g^{ij}(x,p)=\frac{1}{2}\dot{\partial}^i\dot{\partial}^jK^2(x,p)$, is positive definite at all points of $T^{\ast}M_0$. We notice that in fact $K(x,p)>0$, whenever $p\neq0$. The pair $(M,K)$ is called a Cartan space.
nodes.statement_short: A Cartan structure is a positively 1-homogeneous $K$ on $T^{\ast}M$, smooth off the zero section, whose Hessian $(g^{ij})$ is positive definite; $(M,K)$ is a Cartan space.
differentia: (iii) the $n\times n$ matrix $(g^{ij})$, where $g^{ij}(x,p)=\frac{1}{2}\dot{\partial}^i\dot{\partial}^jK^2(x,p)$, is positive definite at all points of $T^{\ast}M_0$

nodes.name: The covectors $p^i$ and the Cartan tensor $C^{ijk}$
nodes.statement: Using this notations, let us define \[ p^i=\frac{1}{2}\dot{\partial}^iK^2\ \ \textrm{and}\ \ C^{ijk}=-\frac{1}{4}\dot{\partial}^i\dot{\partial}^j\dot{\partial}^kK^2. \]

nodes.name: Homogeneity properties of $K$
nodes.statement: The properties of $K$ imply that \begin{eqnarray} &&p^i=g^{ij}p_j,\ \ p_i=g_{ij}p^j,\ \ K^2=g^{ij}p_ip_j=p_ip^j,\nonumber\\ &&C^{ijk}p_k=C^{ikj}p_k=C^{kij}p_k=0. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Raising/lowering indices with $g^{ij}$ is compatible with $p_i$, $K^2=g^{ij}p_ip_j$, and the Cartan tensor is totally $p$-orthogonal.
assumptions: The properties of $K$
conclusions: p^i=g^{ij}p_j,\ \ p_i=g_{ij}p^j,\ \ K^2=g^{ij}p_ip_j=p_ip^j,
C^{ijk}p_k=C^{ikj}p_k=C^{kij}p_k=0.

nodes.name: Formal Christoffel symbols $\gamma^i_{jk}$
nodes.statement: One considers the formal Christoffel symbols by \begin{equation} \gamma^i_{jk}(x,p):=\frac{1}{2}g^{is}(\partial_kg_{js}+\partial_jg_{sk}-\partial_sg_{jk}), \end{equation} and the contractions $\gamma^{\circ}_{jk}(x,p):=\gamma^i_{jk}(x,p)p_i$, $\gamma^{\circ}_{j\circ}:=\gamma^i_{jk}p_ip^k$.

nodes.name: Miron's canonical nonlinear connection $N_{ij}$
nodes.statement: Then the functions \begin{equation} N_{ij}(x,p)=\gamma^{\circ}_{ij}(x,p)-\frac{1}{2}\gamma^{\circ}_{h\circ}(x,p)\dot{\partial}^hg_{ij}(x,p), \end{equation} define a nonlinear connection on $T^{\ast}M$. This nonlinear connection was discovered by R. Miron \cite{Mir1}.
nodes.statement_short: The explicit $N_{ij}$ built from the formal Christoffel symbols defines the canonical nonlinear connection of a Cartan space.

nodes.name: $N$-linear connection
nodes.statement: A linear connection $D$ on $T^{\ast}M$ is said to be an $N$-linear connection if $D$ preserves by parallelism the distribution $N$ and $V$, also we have $D\theta=0$, for $\theta=\delta p_i\wedge dx^i$.
differentia: $D$ preserves by parallelism the distribution $N$ and $V$

nodes.name: Adapted-basis representation of an $N$-linear connection
nodes.statement: One proves that an $N$-linear connection can be represented in the adapted basis $(\delta_i,\dot{\partial}^i)$ in the form \begin{eqnarray} D_{\delta_j}\delta_i\!\!\!\!&=&\!\!\!\!H^k_{ij}\delta_j,\ \ \ D_{\delta_j}\dot{\partial}^i=-H^i_{kj}\dot{\partial}^k,\\ D_{\dot{\partial}^j}\delta_i\!\!\!\!&=&\!\!\!\!V^{kj}_i\delta_k,\ \ \ D_{\dot{\partial}^j}\dot{\partial}^i=-V^{ij}_k\dot{\partial}^k, \end{eqnarray} where $V^{kj}_i$ is a \textit{d}-tensor field and $H^k_{ij}(x,p)$ behave like the coefficients of a linear connection on $M$.
nodes.statement_short: Every $N$-linear connection is encoded in the adapted basis by coefficient pairs $(H^k_{ij},V^{kj}_i)$.
assumptions: an $N$-linear connection
conclusions: can be represented in the adapted basis $(\delta_i,\dot{\partial}^i)$ in the form

nodes.name: $h$- and $v$-covariant derivatives
nodes.statement: The functions $H^k_{ij}$ and $V^{kj}_i$ define operators of \textit{h}-covariant and \textit{v}-covariant derivatives in the algebra of \textit{d}-tensor fields, denoted by $_{|k}$ and $\mid^k$, respectively. For $g^{ij}$ these are given by \begin{eqnarray} {g^{ij}}_{|k}\!\!\!\!&=&\!\!\!\!\delta_kg^{ij}+g^{sj}H^i_{sk}+g^{is}H^j_{sk},\\ g^{ij}\!\!\mid^k\!\!\!\!&=&\!\!\!\!\dot{\partial}^kg^{ij}+g^{sj}V^{ik}_s+g^{is}V^{jk}_s. \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: Metrical $N$-linear connection
nodes.statement: An \textit{N}-linear connection given in the adapted basis $(\delta_i,\dot{\partial}^j)$ as $D\Gamma(N)=(H^i_{jk},V^{ik}_j)$ is called metrical if \begin{equation} {g^{ij}}_{|k}=0,\ \ \ \ g^{ij}\!\!\mid^k=0. \end{equation}
nodes.genus: \textit{N}-linear connection given in the adapted basis $(\delta_i,\dot{\partial}^j)$

nodes.name: Canonical metrical connection $C\Gamma(N)$ of a Cartan space
nodes.statement: One verifies that the \textit{N}-linear connection $C\Gamma(N)=(H^i_{jk},C^{ik}_j)$ with \begin{eqnarray} H^i_{jk}\!\!\!\!&=&\!\!\!\!\frac{1}{2}g^{is}(\delta_jg_{sk}+\delta_kg_{js}-\delta_sg_{jk}),\\ C^{jk}_i\!\!\!\!&=&\!\!\!\!-\frac{1}{2}g_{is}(\dot{\partial}^jg^{sk}+\dot{\partial}^kg^{sj}-\dot{\partial}^sg^{jk})=g_{is}C^{sjk}, \end{eqnarray} is metrical and its \textit{h}-torsion $T^i_{jk}:=H^i_{jk}-H^i_{kj}=0$, \textit{v}-torsion $S^{jk}_i:=C^{jk}_i-C^{kj}_i=0$ and deflection tensor $\Delta_{ij}=N_{ij}-p_kH^k_{ij}=0$. Moreover, it is unique with these properties. This is called the canonical metrical connection of the Cartan space $(M,K)$.
nodes.statement_short: $C\Gamma(N)=(H^i_{jk},C^{ik}_j)$ is the unique metrical $N$-linear connection with vanishing $h$-, $v$-torsion and deflection tensor.
nodes.origin_citation: R. Miron; Miron, Hrimiuc, Shimada & Sabau
assumptions: the \textit{N}-linear connection $C\Gamma(N)=(H^i_{jk},C^{ik}_j)$
conclusions: is metrical and its \textit{h}-torsion $T^i_{jk}:=H^i_{jk}-H^i_{kj}=0$, \textit{v}-torsion $S^{jk}_i:=C^{jk}_i-C^{kj}_i=0$ and deflection tensor $\Delta_{ij}=N_{ij}-p_kH^k_{ij}=0$
Moreover, it is unique with these properties.

nodes.name: Properties of the canonical metrical connection
nodes.statement: It has also the following properties: \begin{eqnarray} K^2_{|j}:\!\!\!\!&=&\!\!\!\!\delta_jK^2=0,\ \ K^2\!\!\mid^j=2p^j,\\ p_{i|j}\!\!\!\!&=&\!\!\!\! p^i_{|j}=0,\ \ p_i\!\!\mid^j=\delta^j_i,\ \ p^i\!\!\mid^j=g^{ij}. \\ R_{kij}p^k\!\!\!\!&=&\!\!\!\!0, \ \ P^i_{jk}p^j=0,\ \ P^i_{jk}:=H^i_{jk}-{\dot{\partial}}^iN_{jk}. \\ \delta_ig_{jk}\!\!\!\!&=&\!\!\!\!H^s_{ji}g_{sk}+H^s_{ki}g_{js}. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: For the Cartan connection $K^2$ is $h$-parallel, $p_i$ and $p^i$ are $h$-parallel, $R_{kij}p^k=0$, $P^i_{jk}p^j=0$ and $\delta_ig_{jk}$ is expressed through $H^s_{ji}$.
assumptions: It has also the following properties:

nodes.name: The energy $\tau$ and the data $(v,\alpha,\beta)$
nodes.statement: Suppose that \begin{equation} \tau :=\frac{1}{2}K^2=\frac{1}{2}g^{ij}(x,p)p_{i}p_{j}, \end{equation} we consider a real valued smooth function $v$ defined on $[0,\infty)\subset {\mathbb R} $ and real constants $\alpha $ and $\beta$.

nodes.name: The $M$-tensor field $G_{ij}$
nodes.statement: We define the following symmetric $M$-tensor field of type (0,2) on $T^{\ast}M_0$ having the components \begin{equation} G_{ij}:=\frac{1}{\beta}g_{ij}+\frac{v(\tau )}{\alpha \beta }p_{i} p_{j}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: A one-parameter deformation of $g_{ij}$ along the momentum directions, $G_{ij}=\frac{1}{\beta}g_{ij}+\frac{v(\tau)}{\alpha\beta}p_ip_j$.

nodes.name: Positive definiteness criterion for $(G_{ij})$
nodes.statement: It follows easily that the matrix $(G_{ij})$ is positive definite if and only if $\alpha ,\beta >0,\, \, \,\, \alpha +2\tau v>0.$
assumptions: we consider a real valued smooth function $v$ defined on $[0,\infty)\subset {\mathbb R} $ and real constants $\alpha $ and $\beta$
conclusions: the matrix $(G_{ij})$ is positive definite if and only if $\alpha ,\beta >0,\, \, \,\, \alpha +2\tau v>0.$

nodes.name: Inverse components $G^{kl}$
nodes.statement: The inverse of this matrix has the entries \begin{equation} G^{kl}=\beta g^{kl}-\frac{v\beta }{\alpha +2\tau v}p^{k} p^{l}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The inverse of $(G_{ij})$ is $G^{kl}=\beta g^{kl}-\frac{v\beta}{\alpha+2\tau v}p^kp^l$.

nodes.name: Positive definiteness of $(G^{kl})$
nodes.statement: The components $G^{kl} $ define symmetric $M$-tensor field of type (0,2) on $T^{\ast}M_0$. It is easy to see that if the matrix $(G_{ij} )$ is positive definite, then matrix $(G^{kl} )$ is positive definite too.
assumptions: if the matrix $(G_{ij} )$ is positive definite
conclusions: matrix $(G^{kl} )$ is positive definite too

nodes.name: The Riemannian metric $G$ on $T^{\ast}M_0$
nodes.statement: Using $(G_{ij})$ and $(G^{ij})$, the following Riemannian metric on $T^{\ast}M_0$ is defined \begin{equation} G=G_{ij}dx^{i}dx^{j}+G^{ij}\delta p_{i}\delta p_{j}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: The almost complex structure $J$ on $T^{\ast}M_0$
nodes.statement: Now, we define an almost complex structure $J$ on $T^{\ast}M_0$ by \begin{equation} J(\delta _{i})=G_{ik}\dot{\partial}^k,\ \ \ J(\dot{\partial}^i)=-G^{ik}\delta _k. \end{equation}

nodes.name: $J$ is an almost complex structure ($J^2=-I$)
nodes.statement: It is easy to check that $J^2=-I$.
assumptions: J(\delta _{i})=G_{ik}\dot{\partial}^k,\ \ \ J(\dot{\partial}^i)=-G^{ik}\delta _k.

nodes.name: $(T^{\ast}M_0,G,J)$ is an almost Kählerian manifold
nodes.statement: $(T^{\ast}M_0,G,J)$ is an almost K\"{a}hlerian manifold.
assumptions: G=G_{ij}dx^{i}dx^{j}+G^{ij}\delta p_{i}\delta p_{j}.
J(\delta _{i})=G_{ik}\dot{\partial}^k,\ \ \ J(\dot{\partial}^i)=-G^{ik}\delta _k.
conclusions: $(T^{\ast}M_0,G,J)$ is an almost K\"{a}hlerian manifold.

nodes.name: Proof that $(T^{\ast}M_0,G,J)$ is almost Kählerian
nodes.statement: Since the matrix $(H^{kl} )$ is the inverse of the matrix $(G_{ij} ),$ then we have \[ G(J\delta_i,J\delta_j)=G_{ik}G_{jr}G(\dot{\partial}^k,\dot{\partial}^r)=G_{ik}G_{jr}G^{kr}=G_{ij}=G(\delta_i,\delta_j). \] The relations \[ G(J\dot{\partial}^i,J\dot{\partial}^j)=G(\dot{\partial}^i,\dot{\partial}^j),\ \ \ \ G(J\delta _i,J\dot{\partial}^j)=G(\delta _i,\dot{\partial}^j)=0, \] may be obtained in a similar way, thus \[ G(JX,JY)=G(X,Y),\, \, \, \, \, \, \, \forall X,Y\in \Gamma(T^{\ast}M_0). \] This means that $G$ is almost Hermitian with respect to $J$. The fundamental 2-form associated by this almost K\"{a}hler structure is $\Omega$, defined by \[ \theta(X,Y):=G(X,JY),\, \, \, \, \forall X,Y\in \Gamma (T^{\ast}M_0). \] Then we get \[ \theta(\dot{\partial}^i,\delta_j)=G(\dot{\partial}^i,J\delta_j)=G(\dot{\partial}^i,G_{jk}\dot{\partial}^k)=G^{ik}G_{jk}=\delta^i_j, \] and \[ \theta(\delta_i,\delta_j)=\theta(\dot{\partial}^i,\dot{\partial}^j)=0. \] Hence, we have \begin{equation} \theta=\delta p_i\wedge dx^i, \end{equation} that is the canonical symplectic form of $T^{\ast}M$.
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation: $G(JX,JY)=G(X,Y)$ on the adapted basis gives almost Hermitian, and the fundamental 2-form equals $\delta p_i\wedge dx^i$, the canonical symplectic form.

nodes.name: Hermitian property on horizontal vectors
nodes.statement: Since the matrix $(H^{kl} )$ is the inverse of the matrix $(G_{ij} ),$ then we have \[ G(J\delta_i,J\delta_j)=G_{ik}G_{jr}G(\dot{\partial}^k,\dot{\partial}^r)=G_{ik}G_{jr}G^{kr}=G_{ij}=G(\delta_i,\delta_j). \]
nodes.statement_short: Compute $G(J\delta_i,J\delta_j)$ using $G_{ik}G_{jr}G^{kr}=G_{ij}$.

nodes.name: Remaining cases and almost Hermitian conclusion
nodes.statement: The relations \[ G(J\dot{\partial}^i,J\dot{\partial}^j)=G(\dot{\partial}^i,\dot{\partial}^j),\ \ \ \ G(J\delta _i,J\dot{\partial}^j)=G(\delta _i,\dot{\partial}^j)=0, \] may be obtained in a similar way, thus \[ G(JX,JY)=G(X,Y),\, \, \, \, \, \, \, \forall X,Y\in \Gamma(T^{\ast}M_0). \] This means that $G$ is almost Hermitian with respect to $J$.
nodes.statement_short: The mixed and vertical cases follow the same way, so $G(JX,JY)=G(X,Y)$, i.e. $G$ is almost Hermitian.

nodes.name: Introduce the fundamental 2-form
nodes.statement: The fundamental 2-form associated by this almost K\"{a}hler structure is $\Omega$, defined by \[ \theta(X,Y):=G(X,JY),\, \, \, \, \forall X,Y\in \Gamma (T^{\ast}M_0). \]
nodes.statement_short: Define $\theta(X,Y):=G(X,JY)$.

nodes.name: Evaluate the 2-form on the adapted basis
nodes.statement: Then we get \[ \theta(\dot{\partial}^i,\delta_j)=G(\dot{\partial}^i,J\delta_j)=G(\dot{\partial}^i,G_{jk}\dot{\partial}^k)=G^{ik}G_{jk}=\delta^i_j, \] and \[ \theta(\delta_i,\delta_j)=\theta(\dot{\partial}^i,\dot{\partial}^j)=0. \]
nodes.statement_short: Only the mixed components survive and equal $\delta^i_j$.

nodes.name: Identify $\theta$ with the canonical symplectic form
nodes.statement: Hence, we have \begin{equation} \theta=\delta p_i\wedge dx^i, \end{equation} that is the canonical symplectic form of $T^{\ast}M$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude $\theta=\delta p_i\wedge dx^i$, which is closed, so the structure is almost Kähler.

nodes.name: Brackets of the adapted frame on a Cartan space
nodes.statement: Let $(M,K)$ be a Cartan space. Then we have the following:\\ $(1)\ \ [\delta_i,\delta_j]=R_{kij}{\dot{\partial}}^k$,\\ $(2)\ \ [\delta_i,{\dot{\partial}}^j]=-({\dot{\partial}}^jN_{ik}){\dot{\partial}}^k$,\\ $(3)\ \ [{\dot{\partial}}^i,{\dot{\partial}}^j]=0$,\\ where $R_{kij}=\delta_jN_{ki}-\delta_iN_{kj}$.
nodes.statement_short: Lie brackets of $\delta_i$ and $\dot{\partial}^i$ are governed by the curvature $R_{kij}$ of the nonlinear connection.
nodes.origin_citation: Miron, Hrimiuc, Shimada & Sabau; Peyghan & Tayebi
assumptions: Let $(M,K)$ be a Cartan space.
conclusions: $(1)\ \ [\delta_i,\delta_j]=R_{kij}{\dot{\partial}}^k$
$(2)\ \ [\delta_i,{\dot{\partial}}^j]=-({\dot{\partial}}^jN_{ik}){\dot{\partial}}^k$
$(3)\ \ [{\dot{\partial}}^i,{\dot{\partial}}^j]=0$

nodes.name: Integrability criterion for $J$
nodes.statement: Let $(M, K)$ be a Cartan space. Then $J$ is a complex structure on $T^{\ast}M_0$ if and only if $A_{kij}=0$ and \begin{equation} R_{kij}=\frac{v}{\alpha\beta^2}(g_{ik}p_j-g_{jk}p_i), \end{equation} where $A_{kij}=\delta_i G_{jk}-\delta_j G_{ik}+G_{ir}{\dot{\partial}}^rN_{jk}-G_{jr}{\dot{\partial}}^rN_{ik}$.
nodes.statement_short: $J$ is integrable exactly when $A_{kij}=0$ and the nonlinear-connection curvature has the special form $R_{kij}=\frac{v}{\alpha\beta^2}(g_{ik}p_j-g_{jk}p_i)$.
assumptions: Let $(M, K)$ be a Cartan space.
conclusions: $J$ is a complex structure on $T^{\ast}M_0$ if and only if $A_{kij}=0$
R_{kij}=\frac{v}{\alpha\beta^2}(g_{ik}p_j-g_{jk}p_i),

nodes.name: Proof of the integrability criterion
nodes.statement: Using the definition of the Nijenhuis tensor field $N_J$ of $J$, that is, \[ N_J(X,Y)=[JX,JY]-J[JX,Y]-J[X,JY]-[X,Y],\ \ \ \forall X, Y\in \Gamma(T^{\ast}M) \] we get \begin{equation} N_J(\delta_i,\delta_j)=A_{hij}H^{hk}\delta_k+ (B_{kij}-R_{kij}){\dot{\partial}}^k, \end{equation} where $B_{kij}=G_{ir}{\dot{\partial}}^rG_{jk}-G_{jr}{\dot{\partial}}^rG_{ik}$. Let $C_{jk}^r:=g_{jl}g_{sk}C^{rls}$, then we have \[ {\dot{\partial}}^rg_{jk}=-g_{jl}g_{sk}{\dot{\partial}}^rg^{ls}=2g_{jl}g_{sk}C^{rls}=2C_{jk}^r. \] By the above equation, we obtain \begin{equation} G_{ir}{\dot{\partial}}^rG_{jk}=\frac{2}{\beta^2}C_{ijk} +\frac{v}{\alpha\beta^2}(g_{ji}p_k+g_{ik}p_j) +(\frac{v^{\prime}}{\alpha\beta^2}+\frac{2vv^{\prime}\tau}{\alpha\beta}+\frac{2v^2}{\alpha^2\beta^2})p_ip_jp_k. \end{equation} where $C_{ijk}=g_{ir}C_{jk}^r$. From (\ref{Nij2}) we get \begin{equation} B_{kij}=\frac{v}{\alpha\beta^2}(g_{ik}p_j-g_{jk}p_i). \end{equation} By a straightforward computation, it follows that $N_J({\dot{\partial}}^i,{\dot{\partial}}^j)=0, N_J({\dot{\partial}}^i,\delta_j)=0$, whenever $N_j(\delta_i,\delta_j)=0$. Therefore, from relations (\ref{Nij1}) and (\ref{Nij3}), we conclude that the necessary and sufficient conditions for vanishing the Nijenhuis tensor field $N_J$ is obtained, so that J is a complex structure. Thus $A_{kij}=0$ and (\ref{2}) hold.
nodes.statement_short: Compute the Nijenhuis tensor in the adapted frame and force it to vanish.

nodes.name: Nijenhuis tensor in the adapted frame
nodes.statement: Using the definition of the Nijenhuis tensor field $N_J$ of $J$, that is, \[ N_J(X,Y)=[JX,JY]-J[JX,Y]-J[X,JY]-[X,Y],\ \ \ \forall X, Y\in \Gamma(T^{\ast}M) \] we get \begin{equation} N_J(\delta_i,\delta_j)=A_{hij}H^{hk}\delta_k+ (B_{kij}-R_{kij}){\dot{\partial}}^k, \end{equation} where $B_{kij}=G_{ir}{\dot{\partial}}^rG_{jk}-G_{jr}{\dot{\partial}}^rG_{ik}$.
nodes.statement_short: Expand $N_J(\delta_i,\delta_j)$ into horizontal part $A_{hij}$ and vertical part $B_{kij}-R_{kij}$.

nodes.name: Introduce $C^r_{jk}$ and differentiate $g_{jk}$
nodes.statement: Let $C_{jk}^r:=g_{jl}g_{sk}C^{rls}$, then we have \[ {\dot{\partial}}^rg_{jk}=-g_{jl}g_{sk}{\dot{\partial}}^rg^{ls}=2g_{jl}g_{sk}C^{rls}=2C_{jk}^r. \]
nodes.statement_short: Set $C^r_{jk}=g_{jl}g_{sk}C^{rls}$ so that $\dot{\partial}^rg_{jk}=2C^r_{jk}$.

nodes.name: Compute $G_{ir}\dot{\partial}^rG_{jk}$
nodes.statement: By the above equation, we obtain \begin{equation} G_{ir}{\dot{\partial}}^rG_{jk}=\frac{2}{\beta^2}C_{ijk} +\frac{v}{\alpha\beta^2}(g_{ji}p_k+g_{ik}p_j) +(\frac{v^{\prime}}{\alpha\beta^2}+\frac{2vv^{\prime}\tau}{\alpha\beta}+\frac{2v^2}{\alpha^2\beta^2})p_ip_jp_k. \end{equation} where $C_{ijk}=g_{ir}C_{jk}^r$.
nodes.statement_short: Differentiate $G_{jk}$ and contract with $G_{ir}$.

nodes.name: Antisymmetrize to obtain $B_{kij}$
nodes.statement: From (\ref{Nij2}) we get \begin{equation} B_{kij}=\frac{v}{\alpha\beta^2}(g_{ik}p_j-g_{jk}p_i).
nodes.statement_short: Antisymmetrizing cancels the $C_{ijk}$ and $p_ip_jp_k$ terms.

nodes.name: Remaining Nijenhuis components vanish
nodes.statement: By a straightforward computation, it follows that $N_J({\dot{\partial}}^i,{\dot{\partial}}^j)=0, N_J({\dot{\partial}}^i,\delta_j)=0$, whenever $N_j(\delta_i,\delta_j)=0$.
nodes.statement_short: The purely vertical and mixed components of $N_J$ vanish once the horizontal-horizontal one does.

nodes.name: Conclude the necessary and sufficient condition
nodes.statement: Therefore, from relations (\ref{Nij1}) and (\ref{Nij3}), we conclude that the necessary and sufficient conditions for vanishing the Nijenhuis tensor field $N_J$ is obtained, so that J is a complex structure. Thus $A_{kij}=0$ and (\ref{2}) hold.
nodes.statement_short: $N_J=0$ iff $A_{kij}=0$ and $B_{kij}=R_{kij}$, i.e. equation (2).

nodes.name: Curvature normalization $R_{kij}=c(g_{jk}p_i-g_{ik}p_j)$
nodes.statement: In equation (\ref{2}), we put $-\frac{v}{\alpha\beta^2}=c$, where $c$ is constant. Then we get \begin{equation} R_{kij}=c(g_{jk}p_i-g_{ik}p_j).
nodes.statement_short: Setting $c=-v/(\alpha\beta^2)$ rewrites the integrability condition as constant-curvature form.

nodes.name: Integrability of $J$ for $n\geq 3$
nodes.statement: Let $(M,K)$ be a Cartan space of dimension $n\geq 3$. Then the almost complex structure $J$ on $T^{\ast}M_0$ is integrable if and only if (\ref{3}) is hold and the function $v$ is given by \begin{equation} v=-c\alpha\beta^2.
nodes.statement_short: For $n\geq3$, $J$ is integrable iff the curvature is of constant type (3) and $v=-c\alpha\beta^2$.
assumptions: Let $(M,K)$ be a Cartan space of dimension $n\geq 3$.
conclusions: the almost complex structure $J$ on $T^{\ast}M_0$ is integrable if and only if (\ref{3}) is hold and the function $v$ is given by
v=-c\alpha\beta^2.

nodes.name: Proof of the integrability theorem
nodes.statement: From equation $p_{i|k}=0$ of relation (\ref{4}), we conclude that $\delta_ip_k=N_{ik}$. Hence the tensor field $A_{kij}$ takes the form $A_{kij}=\delta_i g_{jk}-\delta_j g_{ik}+g_{ir}{\dot{\partial}}^rN_{jk}-g_{jr}{\dot{\partial}}^rN_{ik}$ and by part $(iii)$ of Proposition 2.3 in chapter 7 of \cite{MirHri}, it vanishes for Cartan spaces. Now we let $v=-c\alpha\beta^2$, then from equation $A_{kij}=0$ and Theorem \ref{3.3}, we conclude that $J$ is integrable if and only if (\ref{3}) is hold.
nodes.statement_short: Show $A_{kij}$ reduces to the Cartan-space expression which vanishes, then apply Theorem 3.3 with $v=-c\alpha\beta^2$.

nodes.name: Use $p_{i|k}=0$
nodes.statement: From equation $p_{i|k}=0$ of relation (\ref{4}), we conclude that $\delta_ip_k=N_{ik}$.
nodes.statement_short: Horizontal parallelism of $p_i$ gives $\delta_ip_k=N_{ik}$.

nodes.name: $A_{kij}$ vanishes on Cartan spaces
nodes.statement: Hence the tensor field $A_{kij}$ takes the form $A_{kij}=\delta_i g_{jk}-\delta_j g_{ik}+g_{ir}{\dot{\partial}}^rN_{jk}-g_{jr}{\dot{\partial}}^rN_{ik}$ and by part $(iii)$ of Proposition 2.3 in chapter 7 of \cite{MirHri}, it vanishes for Cartan spaces.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce $A_{kij}$ to its $g$-form and cite Proposition 2.3 of Miron-Hrimiuc for its vanishing.

nodes.name: Apply Theorem 3.3
nodes.statement: Now we let $v=-c\alpha\beta^2$, then from equation $A_{kij}=0$ and Theorem \ref{3.3}, we conclude that $J$ is integrable if and only if (\ref{3}) is hold.
nodes.statement_short: With $A_{kij}=0$ the criterion of Theorem 3.3 reduces to condition (3).

nodes.name: Cartan space of constant scalar $c$
nodes.statement: A Cartan space $K^n$ is of constant scalar $c$ if \begin{equation} H_{hijk}p^ip^jX^hX^k=c(g_{hj}g_{ik}-g_{hk}g_{ij})p^ip^jX^hX^k, \end{equation} for every $(x,p)\in T^{\ast}_0M$ and $X=(X^i)\in T_xM$. Here $H_{hijk}$ is the (hh)h-curvature of the linear Cartan connection of $K^n$.

nodes.name: Constant-curvature relation $R_{hjk}p^j=c(K^2g_{hk}-p_hp_k)$
nodes.statement: We replace $H_{hijk}$ in (\ref{7}) with $g_{is}H^s_{hjk}$ and so it reduce to \begin{equation} p_sH^s_{hjk}p^jX^hX^k=c(p_hp_k-K^2g_{hk})X^hX^k. \end{equation} By part (ii) of Proposition 5.1 in chapter 7 of \cite{MirHri}, $p_sH^s_{hjk}=-R_{hjk}$, hence we get \[ R_{hjk}p^jX^hX^k=c(K^2g_{hk}-p_hp_k)X^hX^k, \] or equivalently \begin{equation} R_{hjk}p^j=c(K^2g_{hk}-p_hp_k), \end{equation} because $(X^h)$ and $X^k$ are arbitrary vector fields on $M$.
nodes.statement_short: Rewriting the constant-scalar condition through $p_sH^s_{hjk}=-R_{hjk}$ yields $R_{hjk}p^j=c(K^2g_{hk}-p_hp_k)$.

nodes.name: Condition (3) implies constant scalar curvature
nodes.statement: It is easy to check that (\ref{8}) follows from (\ref{3}). Hence we conclude that if (\ref{3}) is hold, then Cartan space $K^n$ has the constant scalar curvature $c$.
assumptions: if (\ref{3}) is hold
conclusions: Cartan space $K^n$ has the constant scalar curvature $c$

nodes.name: Kähler structure for constant flag curvature
nodes.statement: Let $(M,K)$ be a Cartan space with constant flag curvature $c$. Suppose that $v$ is given by (\ref{constant}). Then\\ $(i)$ for negative constant $c$, structure $(T^{\ast}M_0,G,J)$ is a K\"{a}hler manifold;\\ $(ii)$ for positive constant $c$, the tube around the zero section in $T^{\ast}M$, defined by the condition $2\tau=K^2<\frac{1}{c\beta^2}$, is a K\"{a}hler manifold.
nodes.statement_short: For $c<0$ the whole $(T^{\ast}M_0,G,J)$ is Kähler; for $c>0$ only the tube $2\tau<1/(c\beta^2)$ is.

$(ii)$ for positive constant $c$, the tube around the zero section in $T^{\ast}M$, defined by the condition $2\tau=K^2<\frac{1}{c\beta^2}$, is a K\"{a}hler manifold.

nodes.name: Kähler Einstein structure forces a Riemannian Cartan space
nodes.statement: Let $(M,K)$ be a Cartan space of constant curvature $c$ and the components of the metric $G$ are given by (\ref{Kahler}). Then the following are hold if and only if $(M,K)$ is reduce to a Riemannian space.\\ $(i)$ for $c<0$, $(T^{\ast}M_0,G,J)$ is a K\"{a}hler Einstein manifold.\\ $(ii)$ for $c>0$, $(T_{\beta}^{\ast}M_0,G,J)$ is a K\"{a}hler Einstein manifold, where $T_{\beta}^{\ast}M_0$ is the tube around the zero section in $TM$ defined by $2\tau<\frac{1}{c\beta^2}$.
nodes.statement_short: $(T^{\ast}M_0,G,J)$ (or its tube for $c>0$) is Kähler Einstein if and only if the Cartan space is Riemannian.
assumptions: Let $(M,K)$ be a Cartan space of constant curvature $c$ and the components of the metric $G$ are given by (\ref{Kahler}).
if and only if $(M,K)$ is reduce to a Riemannian space
conclusions: $(i)$ for $c<0$, $(T^{\ast}M_0,G,J)$ is a K\"{a}hler Einstein manifold.
$(ii)$ for $c>0$, $(T_{\beta}^{\ast}M_0,G,J)$ is a K\"{a}hler Einstein manifold, where $T_{\beta}^{\ast}M_0$ is the tube around the zero section in $TM$ defined by $2\tau<\frac{1}{c\beta^2}$.

nodes.name: Proof of the Kähler Einstein rigidity theorem
nodes.statement_short: Forward: compute all Ricci components and get $Ric=cn\beta G$. Converse: contract $p_kRic(\dot\partial^j,\dot\partial^k)$ and split on $\lambda=0$ (contradiction) versus $\lambda\neq0$ (forces $I^j=0$).

nodes.name: Riemannian reduction of the horizontal curvature
nodes.statement: Let $(M,K)$ be a Cartan space. Then $C^{hi}_k$ and $P^h_{ik}$ are vanish and $H^i_{jk}$ is a function of $(x^h)$. Therefore (\ref{curvature14}) reduce to \begin{equation} K(\delta_i,\delta_j)\delta_k=[R^s_{kji}+c^2\beta^2(p_i\delta^s_j-p_j\delta^s_i)p_k]\delta_s.
nodes.statement_short: Vanishing of $C^{hi}_k$ and $P^h_{ik}$ collapses (curvature14) to a purely horizontal expression.

nodes.name: Identify $R^s_{kji}$
nodes.statement: From Proposition 10.2 in chapter 4 of \cite{MirHri}, we have $R_{kji}=-p_hR^h_{kji}$. Then we get \begin{equation} p_hR^h_{kji}=c(g_{kj}\delta^h_i-g_{ki}\delta^h_j)p_h. \end{equation} Differentiating (\ref{Ricc2}) with respect to $p_s$, taking $p=0$, yields \[ R^s_{kji}=c(g_{kj}\delta^s_i-g_{ki}\delta^s_j). \]
nodes.statement_short: Use $R_{kji}=-p_hR^h_{kji}$ and differentiate at $p=0$ to get the constant-curvature form of $R^s_{kji}$.

nodes.name: Horizontal curvature in terms of $G$
nodes.statement: By putting above equation in (\ref{Ricc1}), it follows that \begin{eqnarray} K(\delta_i,\delta_j)\delta_k\!\!\!\!&=&\!\!\!\!c\beta[(\frac{1}{\beta}g_{kj}-c\beta p_kp_j)\delta^s_i-(\frac{1}{\beta}g_{ki}-c\beta\ p_kp_i)\delta^s_j]\delta_s\nonumber\\ \!\!\!\!&=&\!\!\!\!c\beta(G_{kj}\delta^s_i-G_{ki}\delta^s_j)\delta_s.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the horizontal curvature as $c\beta(G_{kj}\delta^s_i-G_{ki}\delta^s_j)\delta_s$.

nodes.name: Mixed curvature component
nodes.statement: Also from (\ref{curvature17}), we obtain \begin{equation} K({\dot{\partial}}^i,\delta_j)\delta_k=c\beta G_{sk}\delta^i_j{\dot{\partial}}^s.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce (curvature17) to $c\beta G_{sk}\delta^i_j\dot{\partial}^s$.

nodes.name: Horizontal Ricci component
nodes.statement_short: Trace the two components to obtain $Ric(\delta_j,\delta_k)=cn\beta G(\delta_j,\delta_k)$.

nodes.name: Vertical Ricci component
nodes.statement:
Similarly from (ef{Curvature6}) and (ef{curvature13}), respectively, we have  egin{eqnarray} K({\dot{\partial}}^i,{\dot{\partial}}^j){\dot{\partial}}^k=c eta(G^{jk}\delta^i_s-G^{ik}\delta^j_s){\dot{\partial}}^s, \end{eqnarray} and  egin{eqnarray} K(\delta_i,{\dot{\partial}}^j){\dot{\partial}}^k=c eta G^{ks}\delta^j_i\delta_s. \end{eqnarray} Using (ef{Ricc6}) and (ef{Ricc7}), we conclude that  egin{eqnarray} Ric({\dot{\partial}}^j,{\dot{\partial}}^k)\!\!\!\!&=&\!\!\!\!G^{ih}G(K(\delta_i,{\dot{\partial}}^j){\dot{\partial}}^k,\delta_h) +G_{ih}G(K({\dot{\partial}}^i,{\dot{\partial}}^j){\dot{\partial}}^k,{\dot{\partial}}^h)
onumber\ \!\!\!\!&=&\!\!\!\!c eta G^{ks}\delta^j_iG^{ih}G_{hs}+c eta(G^{jk}\delta^i_s-G^{ik}\delta^j_s)G_{hi}G^{hs}
onumber\ 
onumber\!\!\!\!&=&\!\!\!\!cn eta G^{jk}\ \!\!\!\!&=&\!\!\!\!cn eta G({\dot{\partial}}^j,{\dot{\partial}}^k).
nodes.statement_short: The same trace on vertical vectors gives $Ric(\dot\partial^j,\dot\partial^k)=cn\beta G(\dot\partial^j,\dot\partial^k)$.

nodes.name: Mixed Ricci component vanishes
nodes.statement: By (\ref{curvature13}) and (\ref{curvature15}),respectively, we have \begin{equation} K(\delta_i,\delta_j){\dot{\partial}}^k=(R^k_{sij}+c\beta R_{hij}G^{hk}p_s){\dot{\partial}}^s, \end{equation} and \begin{equation} K({\dot{\partial}}^i,\delta_j){\dot{\partial}}^k=-c\beta G^{ks}\delta^i_j\delta_s. \end{equation} Using (\ref{Ricc9}) and (\ref{Ricc10}), we obtain \begin{equation} Ric(\delta_j,{\dot{\partial}}^k)=G^{ih}G(K(\delta_i,\delta_j){\dot{\partial}}^k,\delta_h) +G_{ih}G(K({\dot{\partial}}^i,\delta_j){\dot{\partial}}^k,{\dot{\partial}}^h)=0.
nodes.statement_short: $Ric(\delta_j,\dot\partial^k)=0$.

nodes.name: Opposite mixed Ricci component vanishes
nodes.statement: From (\ref{curvature16}), we have \begin{equation} K({\dot{\partial}}^i,{\dot{\partial}}^j)\delta_k=c\beta(G^{is}\delta^j_k-G^{js}\delta^i_k)\delta_s. \end{equation} By attention to (\ref{Ricc4}) and (\ref{Ricc12}), one can obtains \begin{equation} Ric({\dot{\partial}}^j,\delta_k)=G^{ih}G(K(\delta_i,{\dot{\partial}}^j)\delta_k,\delta_h) +G_{ih}G(K({\dot{\partial}}^i,{\dot{\partial}}^j)\delta_k,{\dot{\partial}}^h)=0.
nodes.statement_short: $Ric(\dot\partial^j,\delta_k)=0$.

nodes.name: Conclude the Einstein property
nodes.statement: From (\ref{Ricc5}), (\ref{Ricc8}), (\ref{Ricc11}) and (\ref{Ricc13}), we deduce that \[ Ric(X,Y)=cn\beta G(X,Y),\ \ \ \forall X, Y\in\chi(T^{\ast}M). \] This means that $(T^{\ast}M,G)$ is a Einstein manifold.
nodes.statement_short: Assemble the four cases into $Ric=cn\beta G$.

nodes.name: Set up the converse
nodes.statement: Conversely, suppose that the conditions $(i), (ii)$ are hold. Then there exists a real constant $\lambda$ such that $Ric(X,Y)=\lambda G(X,Y)$. We consider the following cases:
nodes.statement_short: Assume $Ric=\lambda G$ for a real constant $\lambda$ and split on $\lambda$.

nodes.name: Case $\lambda=0$ gives a contradiction
nodes.statement: \textbf{Case (1)}. If $\lambda=0$ (i.e., $(T^{\ast}M,G)$ is Ricci flat), then we have $Ric({\dot{\partial}}^j,{\dot{\partial}}^k)=0$. By using (\ref{Curvature6}),(\ref{curvature13}) and definition of Ricci tensor, we obtain \begin{eqnarray} 0=p_kRic({\dot{\partial}}^j,{\dot{\partial}}^k)=cn\beta p_kG^{jk}- p_kC^{jk,s}_s\!\!\!\!&+&\!\!\!\!\frac{\beta^2}{2}\delta_s(P^j_{rl}g^{lk}g^{sr})p_k +\frac{\beta^2}{2}\delta_s(P^k_{rl}g^{lj}g^{sr})p_k\nonumber\\ \!\!\!\!&+&\!\!\!\! \frac{\beta^2}{2}g^{ts}p_k(P^j_{mt}H^k_{sh}g^{mh}+P^h_{mt}H^k_{sh}g^{mj}). \end{eqnarray} Since $P^j_{rl}g^{lk}g^{sr}p_k=P^j_{rl}p^lg^{sr}=0$ and $\delta_sp_k=H^h_{sk}p_h$, then we have \begin{eqnarray*} \delta_s(P^j_{rl}g^{lk}g^{sr})p_k\!\!\!\!&=&\!\!\!\!-(\delta_sp_k)P^j_{rl}g^{lk}g^{sr}\\ \!\!\!\!&=&\!\!\!\!-P^j_{rl}g^{lk}g^{sr}H^h_{sk}p_h. \end{eqnarray*} Replacing $h$ and $k$, changing $r$ to $t$, and $l$ to $m$ in the above equation yields \begin{equation} \delta_s(P^j_{rl}g^{lk}g^{sr})p_k=-P^j_{tm}g^{mh}g^{st}H^k_{sh}p_k. \end{equation} Similarly, we have \begin{equation} \delta_s(P^k_{rl}g^{lj}g^{sr})p_k=-P^h_{tm}g^{mj}g^{st}H^k_{sh}p_k. \end{equation} With direct computation, we get \begin{eqnarray} \nonumber cn\beta p_kG^{jk}\!\!\!\!&=&\!\!\!\!cn\beta p_k(\beta g^{jk}+\frac{c\beta^3}{1-2c\beta^2\tau}p^jp^k)\\ \!\!\!\!&=&\!\!\!\!\frac{cn\beta^2}{1-2c\beta^2\tau}p^j, \end{eqnarray} and \begin{equation} p_kC^{jk,s}_s=-p^{,s}_kC^{jk}_s=-\delta^s_kC^{jk}_s=-C^{js}_s=-I^j. \end{equation} By using (\ref{Ricc14})-(\ref{Ricc18}), we obtain \begin{equation} \frac{cn\beta^2}{1-2c\beta^2\tau}p^j+I^j=0. \end{equation} Since $p_jI^j=0$, then by contracting (\ref{Ricc19}) with $p_j$, we have \begin{equation} \frac{2cn\beta^2\tau}{1-2c\beta^2\tau}=0. \end{equation} From the above equation, we conclude that $\beta=0$ and this is a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Ricci-flatness forces $\beta=0$, which is impossible.

nodes.name: Case $\lambda\neq0$ forces $I^j=0$
nodes.statement: \textbf{Case (2)}. If $\lambda\neq0$, then we have \[ p_kRic({\dot{\partial}}^j,{\dot{\partial}}^k)=\lambda G^{jk}p_k. \] Therefore by using (\ref{Curvature6}), (\ref{curvature13}), (\ref{Ricc15})-(\ref{Ricc18}), we obtain \begin{equation} I^j=(\lambda-cn\beta)\frac{\beta}{1-2c\beta^2\tau}p^j. \end{equation} By contracting (\ref{Ricc21}) with $p_j$, we have \begin{equation} (\lambda-cn\beta)\frac{2\beta\tau}{1-2c\beta^2\tau}=0, \end{equation} i.e., $\lambda=cn\beta$. Then from (\ref{Ricc21}), we result that $I^j=0$, i.e., $(M,K)$ is reduce to a Riemannian space.
nodes.statement_short: Contracting with $p_j$ gives $\lambda=cn\beta$, hence the mean Cartan torsion $I^j$ vanishes and $K$ is Riemannian.

nodes.name: No non-Riemannian Cartan structure is Einstein
nodes.statement: There is not exist any non-Riemannian Cartan structure such that $(T^{\ast}M_0, G, J)$ became a Einstein manifold.
conclusions: There is not exist any non-Riemannian Cartan structure such that $(T^{\ast}M_0, G, J)$ became a Einstein manifold.

nodes.statement: Let $(M,K)$ be a Cartan space of constant curvature $c$ and the components of the metric $G$ are given by (\ref{Kahler}). Then the following are hold if and only if $(M,K)$ is reduce to a Riemannian space.\\ $(i)$ for $c<0$, $(T^{\ast}M_0,G,J)$ is a locally symmetric K\"{a}hler manifold.\\ $(ii)$ for $c>0$, $(T_{\beta}^{\ast}M_0,G,J)$ is a locally symmetric K\"{a}hler manifold, where $T_{\beta}^{\ast}M_{\circ}$ is the tube around the zero section in $T^{\ast}M$, defined by the condition $2\tau<\frac{1}{c\beta^2}$.
nodes.statement_short: $(T^{\ast}M_0,G,J)$ (or its tube for $c>0$) is a locally symmetric Kähler manifold if and only if the Cartan space is Riemannian.
assumptions: Let $(M,K)$ be a Cartan space of constant curvature $c$ and the components of the metric $G$ are given by (\ref{Kahler}).
if and only if $(M,K)$ is reduce to a Riemannian space

$(ii)$ for $c>0$, $(T_{\beta}^{\ast}M_0,G,J)$ is a locally symmetric K\"{a}hler manifold, where $T_{\beta}^{\ast}M_{\circ}$ is the tube around the zero section in $T^{\ast}M$, defined by the condition $2\tau<\frac{1}{c\beta^2}$.

nodes.statement_short: Forward: all twelve covariant derivatives of the curvature vanish. Converse: contract $\nabla K=0$ to get $2(1-c\beta^2\tau)C^{kus}=0$, hence $C^{kus}=0$.

nodes.name: Forward direction: twelve vanishing cases
nodes.statement: Let $(M,K)$ be a Cartan space. Using (\ref{Curvature6}), (\ref{curvature13})-(\ref{curvature17}), we have computed the covariant derivatives of curvature tensor field $K$ in the local adapted frame $(\delta_i,\dot{\partial}^i)$ with respect to the connection $\nabla$ and obtained in the twelve cases the result is zero.
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation of $\nabla K$ in the adapted frame gives zero in all twelve cases.

nodes.name: Converse setup and decomposition of $\nabla K$
nodes.statement:
Conversely, let $(i)$ and $(ii)$ are hold. Thus we get $
abla K=0$. For simplify, we let $(M,K)$ be a Berwald-Cartan space. Put \[ (
abla K)({\dot{\partial}}^u,{\dot{\partial}}^i,\delta_j,{\dot{\partial}}^k)=M^{uiks}_j\delta_s+N^{uik}_{sj}{\dot{\partial}}^s. \] Since $(
abla K)({\dot{\partial}}^u,{\dot{\partial}}^i,\delta_j,{\dot{\partial}}^k)=0$, then we have $M^{uiks}_j=N^{uik}_{sj}=0$. Thus we have $p^jp_iM^{uiks}_j=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $\nabla K=0$ on a Berwald-Cartan space and split $(\nabla K)$ into horizontal $M$ and vertical $N$ parts.

nodes.name: Expand the contracted horizontal part
nodes.statement: By a straightforward calculation, we obtain \begin{eqnarray} p^jp_iM^{uiks}_j=p^jp_iC^{ks,i,u}_j\!\!\!\!&-&\!\!\!\!2c\beta\tau(G^{ks,u}+G^{kh}C^{us}_h+G^{uh}C^{ks}_h+G^{hs}C^{uk}_h)\nonumber\\ \!\!\!\!&+&\!\!\!\! 2c^2\beta^2\tau(G^{us}G^{kh}+G^{uk}G^{hs})p_h.
nodes.statement_short: Write $p^jp_iM^{uiks}_j$ in terms of $C$ and $G$.

nodes.name: Compute the auxiliary $G$-derivatives
nodes.statement: By a direct computation, we have \begin{equation} G^{ks,u}=-2\beta C^{ksu}+\frac{2c^2\beta^5}{(1-2c\beta^2\tau)^2}p^kp^up^s+\frac{c\beta^3}{1-2c\beta^2\tau}g^{ku}p^s+\frac{c\beta^3}{1-2c\beta^2\tau}g^{su}p^k. \end{equation} Also, we obtain \begin{equation} G^{us}G^{kh}p_h=\frac{\beta}{1-2c\beta^2\tau}p^sG^{ku}=\frac{\beta^2}{1-2c\beta^2\tau}g^{ku}p^s+\frac{c\beta^4}{(1-2c\beta^2\tau)^2}p^up^kp^s, \end{equation} and \begin{equation} G^{uk}G^{hs}p_h=\frac{\beta}{1-2c\beta^2\tau}p^kG^{su}=\frac{\beta^2}{1-2c\beta^2\tau}g^{su}p^k+\frac{c\beta^4}{(1-2c\beta^2\tau)^2}p^up^sp^k.
nodes.statement_short: Evaluate $G^{ks,u}$ and the two contractions $G^{us}G^{kh}p_h$, $G^{uk}G^{hs}p_h$.

nodes.name: Substitute and simplify
nodes.statement: Putting (\ref{symmetric2}), (\ref{symmetric3}) and (\ref{symmetric4}) in (\ref{symmetric1}), one can yields \begin{equation} p^jp_iM^{uiks}_j=p^jp_iC^{ks,i,u}_j-2c\beta\tau(-2\beta C^{kus}+G^{kh}C^{us}_h+G^{uh}C^{ks}_h+G^{hs}C^{uk}_h).
nodes.statement_short: The $p^up^kp^s$ and $g$-terms cancel, leaving a purely Cartan-tensor expression.

nodes.name: Reduce the Cartan-tensor contractions
nodes.statement: Since $p_iC^{ks,i}_j=-C^{ks}_j$, then we obtain \[ p^jp_iC^{ks,i,u}_j=2g^{uj}C^{ks}_j=2C^{kus}. \] Also, since $C^{us}_hp^h=0$, then we have \[ G^{kh}C^{us}_h=G^{uh}C^{ks}_h=G^{hs}C^{uk}_h=\beta C^{kus}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Use $p_iC^{ks,i}_j=-C^{ks}_j$ and $C^{us}_hp^h=0$ to express every contraction through $C^{kus}$.

nodes.name: Final identity
nodes.statement: Therefore (\ref{symmetric5}) reduces to following \begin{equation} p^jp_iM^{uiks}_j=2(1-c\beta^2\tau)C^{kus}.
nodes.statement_short: Everything collapses to $p^jp_iM^{uiks}_j=2(1-c\beta^2\tau)C^{kus}$.

nodes.name: Conclude $K$ is Riemannian
nodes.statement: Since $p^jp_iM^{uiks}_j=0$, then by (\ref{symmetric6}), we have $C^{kus}=0$, i.e., $K$ is a Riemannian metric.
nodes.statement_short: Vanishing of the left-hand side forces the Cartan tensor to vanish.

nodes.name: No non-Riemannian Cartan structure is locally symmetric
nodes.statement: There is not exist any non-Riemannian Cartan structure such that $(T^{\ast}M_0, G, J)$ became a locally symmetric manifold.
conclusions: There is not exist any non-Riemannian Cartan structure such that $(T^{\ast}M_0, G, J)$ became a locally symmetric manifold.
